title: ChirpNeighbors — Bird Facts and Measurement References
scope: 18 proposed San Diego core species plus Blue Jay and Northern Cardinal for the general pack. These are source-cited learning facts, not home sightings.

measurement_policy.length: Retain the source label Length. Cornell and Audubon species measurement blocks do not explicitly define anatomical endpoints. source_endpoint_definition is null. Bill-tip-to-tail-tip is a common field-guide convention, not an explicit definition established by these cited profiles. Do not call these values body-only length.
measurement_policy.wingspan: Retain source label Wingspan; conventionally the spread wingtip-to-wingtip distance, but the cited blocks do not detail posture or measurement protocol. It is not wing chord.
measurement_policy.mass: Source Weight values expressed in grams are recorded as mass; conditions, age and sample sizes are not supplied in the measurement blocks.
measurement_policy.points_and_ranges: Published points remain points. They are not invented ranges, means or medians. Published ranges are source-specific summaries, not guaranteed population extrema or confidence intervals.
measurement_policy.sex_age: Both Sexes is retained only where Cornell labels it. No nestling/fledgling dimensions are inferred. Sex-specific Mourning Dove fields remain separate.
measurement_policy.rendering: No scale factor, body-to-tail ratio or sprite bounding-box size is inferred. Calibration requires an explicitly defined anatomical landmark measurement and a matching, consistently posed asset. Wingspan must never substitute for length.

content_policy: Original paraphrases only; no third-party image, audio or video copied. Fictional personalities are explicitly separate and unset.

facts.name: Anna's Hummingbird
facts.identification: Green-backed, gray below; adult males have a rose-red iridescent crown and throat. Females and young lack the full male display.
facts.behavior: Hovers at flowers, darts between perches and catches tiny arthropods.

fun_facts.text: The male’s colorful throat can look dark when the light hits from a different angle.
Cold conditions can trigger energy-saving torpor.

facts.name: House Finch
facts.identification: Streaked brown finch with a thick curved-profile bill. Adult males often have red on the head and breast; females are brown-streaked.
facts.behavior: Feeds socially and cracks seeds with its stout bill.

fun_facts.text: Male red, orange or yellow tones depend on dietary pigments acquired during molt.
Parents feed their nestlings plant foods, unlike many seed-eating songbirds that give chicks insects.

facts.name: Lesser Goldfinch
facts.identification: Tiny finch; local adult males have a black cap, green back and yellow underside. Females are duller, with pale wingbars.
facts.habitat: yards with seedheads and nearby water
facts.behavior: Clings to seed-bearing plants and feeds in mixed flocks.

fun_facts.text: Males vary geographically: green backs dominate the West Coast, while black-backed males occur elsewhere.
Foraging flocks often mingle with other finch and sparrow species.

facts.name: Black Phoebe
facts.identification: Sooty head and breast contrast with a white belly; slim bill, upright stance and frequent tail pumping.
facts.habitat: open yard/lawn, low perches; water/mud nearby
facts.diet: flying insects; not a seed-feeder bird
facts.behavior: Scans from a low perch, pumps its tail and sallies out after insects.

fun_facts.text: It sometimes catches small fish despite being mainly an insect eater.
Males show females possible nest sites, but the female chooses and builds.

facts.name: California Towhee
facts.identification: Plain brown, long-tailed and stout-billed, with rusty color below the tail; sexes look alike.
facts.behavior: Stays close to cover while hopping, scratching and feeding on the ground.

fun_facts.text: California and Canyon Towhees were once grouped under the name Brown Towhee.
Poison oak can provide both nesting cover and berries for this bird; that is not a recommendation for people to handle the plant.

facts.name: Mourning Dove
facts.identification: Buff-brown dove with black wing spots and a long pointed tail; its head looks small beside its rounded body.
facts.behavior: Walks and picks up seeds on the ground; flies with rapid wingbeats.

fun_facts.text: Seeds can be stored in an expandable food-storage organ called the crop before digestion.
A tight three-bird flight can be a social display involving a pair and another male.

facts.name: Northern Mockingbird
facts.identification: Slender gray bird with pale underparts, a long tail and conspicuous white patches in the wings.
facts.behavior: Sings from exposed perches and runs across open ground.

fun_facts.text: Males can keep learning new sounds throughout life.
Its white-wing flashing is real, but its function remains uncertain; startling insects is a hypothesis.

facts.name: California Scrub-Jay
facts.identification: Crestless blue-and-gray jay with a long tail, white eyebrow and partial blue breast band; young birds are grayer.
facts.diet: acorns, seeds, insects and other foods
facts.behavior: Hops through shrubs and trees and stores food in caches.

fun_facts.text: It sometimes removes ticks from mule deer.
It caches acorns and can steal food it watched other jays hide.

facts.name: Bushtit
facts.identification: Very small gray-brown bird with a short bill and long tail; coastal birds tend to have browner crowns.
facts.behavior: Moves through foliage in busy flocks, sometimes hanging upside down.

fun_facts.text: A nesting pair may receive help from additional adults, often males.
Families can sleep together inside their hanging nest during breeding.

facts.name: American Crow
facts.identification: All black, with a broad fan-shaped tail in flight; smaller-billed and less shaggy-throated than a Common Raven.
facts.behavior: Walks while foraging and gathers socially, including communal roosts.

fun_facts.text: Young birds often help their parents raise later broods.
Winter roosts can gather many families into very large communal groups.

facts.name: Common Raven
facts.identification: Large black bird with a thick bill, shaggy throat and wedge-shaped tail in flight.
facts.habitat: open inland/rural edges and urban opportunities
facts.behavior: Walks and scavenges on the ground and often soars overhead.

fun_facts.text: Young ravens have been observed dropping sticks and catching them in midair.
Ravens can imitate other birds; captive individuals can also learn human sounds.

facts.name: Nuttall's Woodpecker
facts.identification: Small black-and-white woodpecker with a barred back and patterned face; adult males have red at the rear of the crown.
facts.behavior: Clings to trunks and branches while searching for arthropods.

fun_facts.text: Its oak association does not make it an acorn specialist; its diet centers on arthropods.
The species was named for naturalist Thomas Nuttall in 1843.

facts.behavior: Hops and scratches near cover, often joining winter feeding flocks.

fun_facts.text: Young males learn from the local song environment, helping create regional dialects.
Some males living where two song dialects meet can sing both.

facts.name: Hooded Oriole
facts.identification: Long-tailed oriole with a slender curved bill; southwestern adult males are bright yellow with black face/throat and wings, while females are duller.

facts.behavior: Searches leaves and flowers, sometimes hanging beneath foliage.

fun_facts.text: Females can stitch a hanging nest to the underside of a palm leaf using plant fibers.
Although chiefly a warm-season visitor, a few remain in southern California through winter.

facts.name: Bewick's Wren
facts.identification: Brown above and pale gray below, with a bold white eyebrow and a long often-cocked tail; sexes look alike.

fun_facts.text: Young males learn songs from nearby adults and develop their own lasting variations.
The bird is named for engraver Thomas Bewick.

facts.name: Spotted Towhee
facts.identification: Long-tailed sparrow with white wing/back spots, rufous flanks and white belly; males are darker above than females.
facts.habitat: dense brush/leaf litter, canyon or woodland edge
facts.behavior: Scratches backward with both feet in leaf litter.

fun_facts.text: Its backward two-foot scratch exposes food hidden in leaf litter.
It and the Eastern Towhee were formerly treated as one species, the Rufous-sided Towhee.

facts.name: Blue Jay
facts.region_scope: general North America pack; not San Diego native/default
facts.identification: Crested jay with blue, white and black markings and a broad tail; distinct from the crestless California Scrub-Jay.
facts.habitat: woodland edges, oak-rich parks and towns within its range
facts.season: year-round in much of its range, with partial migration; not a San Diego default
facts.diet: nuts, seeds, insects and other animal foods
facts.behavior: Hops and perches; handles seeds/nuts with bill and feet

fun_facts.text: Its blue appearance comes from feather structure interacting with light, not blue pigment.
It can imitate hawk calls; the purpose of this mimicry is not settled.

facts.name: Northern Cardinal
facts.region_scope: general North America pack; not San Diego native/default
facts.identification: Crested bird with a stout orange-red bill; males are red, females brown with red highlights and a dark face patch.
facts.habitat: dense shrubs, gardens, parks and woodland edges within its range
facts.season: generally resident within its range; not a San Diego default
facts.behavior: Forages near the ground and in low cover; pairs often stay together

fun_facts.text: Females sing as well as males, including from the nest.
Both sexes may challenge their reflections while defending territory.
